title: Stairs, hop-ups and step ladders
audience: Operatives and supervisors who clean stairs, landings and lift lobbies, or who reach high points with hop-ups and step ladders.
learningOutcomes: Identify the falls hazards on stairs, landings and steps, and the falls hazards from hop-ups and step ladders.
Choose the lowest-risk way to reach a high point before using any step equipment.
Inspect a hop-up or step ladder before use and withdraw it when it is defective.
Explain why only people holding training and authorisation may work from height.

instruction.heading: Stairs, landings and steps
instruction.body: A falls hazard on stairs comes from a missed step, a slippery nosing, a loose stair rod, debris on a landing, or a load carried in a way that blocks sight of the next step. The register treats stair cleaning as a job with its own written plan, so the stair work must follow that plan and not memory. Stair and landing spaces are used with the handrail in hand, and the lift is used where it is the approved access route for the task and the load. Stair and landing lighting is checked before work starts. Bulk items, bins and equipment are not stored on stairs or landings, because they force people to step around them. A damaged stair, handrail or tread is reported to the supervisor and the facilities team, and the affected section stays closed until it is checked. The building owner or duty holder is responsible for maintaining the stairs; the crew's duty is to report and to keep the stairs clear.

instruction.heading: Hop-ups and step ladders
instruction.body: A hop-up or step ladder is used only if the high point cannot be reached safely from the ground, using long-handled or extension equipment. Before any use, inspect the equipment for cracks, bent or missing steps, loose hinges or locks, worn feet and damage to the platform. Equipment that is defective is withdrawn from use, tagged as not fit for use and reported. Set the equipment on a firm, level surface, open and locked where it has a locking mechanism, and do not place it on a box, a chair, a trolley or any other unstable base to gain height. Do not stand on the top step or the platform the equipment is not designed for. Keep three points of contact where possible, and do not overreach. A second person is nearby when the task is at a height the register requires supervision for. WARNING: Never use a chair, a bin or a stacked item to reach higher.

instruction.heading: Authorisation and the standard named in the register
instruction.body: Elevated work is done only by people who hold training and authorisation from the business for that equipment and that height. This lesson does not authorise anyone to do elevated work and is not a licence or a certificate for that work. The register cites a South African standard for elevated-work equipment, which does not apply in Australia and is not carried into this lesson.

procedure: Check whether the high point can be reached from the ground with extension equipment, and choose that option first.
Confirm the stair work is covered by its own written plan.
Inspect the hop-up or step ladder before use, and withdraw and label it if it is defective.
Set the equipment on a firm, level base and keep the area clear of people and loads.
Work with three points of contact where possible, and do not overreach or stand on an unsuitable step.
Report any damaged stair, handrail or tread, and close the affected section until it is checked.

workedExamples.situation: A crew member must dust a high air vent beside a stair landing, and the only equipment within reach is a step ladder that has a cracked tread.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Decide whether the step ladder is used, state the first action and the record that follows.
workedExamples.reasoning: The cracked tread makes the step ladder defective, so it is withdrawn, tagged as not fit for use and reported. The first option to try is extension equipment from the ground. If the job still needs height, a supervisor confirms that the operative is authorised, and a supplied step ladder that has passed inspection is used on a firm base. The record shows the defect, the label, the report and the method used for the vent.

equipmentAndPpe: Extension and long-handled cleaning equipment for ground-level reach
Inspected hop-up or step ladder supplied by the business, with a visible inspection tag
Labels for defective equipment and the reporting form

commonErrors.error: Standing on a chair or a bin to reach a high point.
commonErrors.prevention: Never use an unstable base. Use extension equipment or an inspected step ladder.

commonErrors.error: Using equipment that has not been inspected, or that was defective and not labelled.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect before every use and withdraw and label any defective equipment straight away.

commonErrors.error: Carrying a bulk item across a landing because the lift is slow.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the approved route and lift for the load, and keep stairs and landings clear.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: WARNING: Only people holding training and authorisation for elevated work may use a hop-up or step ladder for that task. Completing this lesson does not make anyone authorised.

Licence notice: some access equipment and elevated work may fall under licensing or specific authorisation rules in a state or territory. This lesson does not grant a licence, a certificate or any authority for that work. Confirm the work health and safety duties on this point with the regulator in the state or territory where the work is done.
Check the Australian standard for step ladders and hop-ups before use. The register cites a South African standard, which is not carried into this lesson.

qualityStandard: Ground-level options were considered before any step equipment was chosen.
Equipment was inspected before use, and defective equipment was withdrawn, labelled and reported.
Stairs were used with the handrail, kept clear, and any damaged section was closed until checked.
documentationEvidence: Inspection record for step equipment, with the date and inspector
Defect report and withdrawal label where equipment was unfit
Authorisation record showing who may elevated work at the site
summary: Reach high points from the ground first, using extension equipment.
Inspect any hop-up or step ladder before use, and withdraw defective equipment.
Only people holding training and authorisation do elevated work, and this lesson does not authorise anyone.
Keep stairs clear, use the handrail and report any damaged stair section.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before using a step ladder, what should the operative do first?
options: Inspect it and confirm it is the supplied, inspected equipment.
Stand on the top step to reach further and lean out a bit
Place it on the nearest chair to add height and stand on it carefully

knowledgeChecks.question: Who may work from a hop-up for a task at height?
options: Anyone in a hurry to finish the job who is near the van today
Only people trained and authorised by the business for elevated work.
The newest crew member without any training, so they can learn on it

knowledgeChecks.question: A stair handrail is found loose. What should happen?
options: Use the stairs anyway and tell the supervisor at the end of the shift today
Tape it in place and continue and keep the stairs open to all staff and visitors today
Report it immediately and keep people off the affected section until it has been checked.
